newsitem.title: USA: Americans reading, heeding ultraviolet index.
newsitem.headline: Americans reading, heeding ultraviolet index.

text.p: Americans were heeding government forecasts of ultraviolet exposure and reducing their risk of skin cancer by staying out of direct sunlight, federal health officials said Thursday.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said 64 percent of 700 people surveyed were aware that the National Weather Service issues Ultraviolet Index forecasts. The rating from zero to 10 offers a guide to the need for sun protection.
It found that 90 percent of people who had heard or read about the UVI were able to explain it accurately. People in their 40s or 50s were more likely to know about the index.

Of those who were aware of the index, 38 percent said the forecasts had prompted them or a family member to change their exposure to the sun. Most often, the change was "staying out of direct sunlight as much as possible," the survey said.

UVI forecasts are widely available in 58 cities where they are issued daily. "Seventy percent of the weathercasters televise it on a daily basis and 61 percent of newspapers report it," Mia Zmud of the Environmental Protection Agency said.
The CDC said it had the same UVI forecast percentages.

Health officials said skin cancer can occur after chronic exposure to the sun or after repeated sunburns. Skin cancer is the most common and most rapidly increasing form of cancer and 20 percent of Americans will develop it in their lifetime.

The CDC recommends that people who are directly exposed to the sun during the day should wear a broad-brimmed hat, protective clothing and sunglasses to reduce exposure and use sunscreen lotion with a sun protection factor of at least 15.
